notes:
These are verse-by-verse notes on Colossians 4, drawn only from the pages I read. Each point is followed by its URL.

**A few things to know first.** I didn't find a Protestant tradition's own teacher openly disagreeing with another tradition on any verse. The real disagreements I found are about two questions: who wrote or received "the letter from Laodicea" (v. 16), and whether Nympha was a woman (v. 15). The commentators on those questions come from mixed traditions. I didn't find any material from prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teachers. I also couldn't read the Pulpit Commentary in full, Wesley's notes, or anything from oca.org, Lutheran sites or Pentecostal denominational sites.

---

**v. 1**
- Gill thinks this verse really belongs to chapter 3. He finds it strange that the chapter break was put here, since the verse finishes the instructions to slaves and masters and has no link to what follows. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/colossians/4.htm
- For Gill, "just and equal" means proper food and clothing, wages owed by law or agreement, gentle treatment, care in sickness, fair correction, and no favourites. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/colossians/4.htm
- Ellicott says the word translated "equal" can mean "equity" or "equality." The former is far commoner (especially in connection with justice), and probably all that is intended here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/4.htm
- Catholic/Orthodox (Chrysostom): "just" and "equal" mean keeping slaves well supplied so they don't depend on others, and paying them back for their work. "You also have a Master" puts masters under the same service as their slaves. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230310.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik (Enduring Word) says the Greek word behind "devote yourselves" means "to be strong." It implies steady, fervent prayer, not sleepy praying. Following N.T. Wright, he sees a three-part pattern: intercession, watching for answers, and thanksgiving when answers appear. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-4/
- Gill: this is addressed to the whole church. It doesn't mean praying formally all the time; it means praying often and steadily, so that no day passes without prayer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/colossians/4.htm
- Precept Austin: the command is in the present tense, which calls for ongoing devotion to prayer. https://www.preceptaustin.org/colossians_chap_4_word_study
- Chrysostom: Paul adds "watching" because long praying makes people listless. They should give thanks for every kind of benefit, including suffering. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230310.htm

**v. 3**
- Ellicott: in 1 Corinthians 16:9 an "open door" means an outward opportunity. here the "door of utterance" is the removal of all internal impediments to preaching. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/4.htm
- Gill allows both readings: an opportunity to preach and open hearts in the hearers, or freedom of speech for Paul himself. He notes Paul asks for the door of the word to open, not the prison door. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/colossians/4.htm
- Guzik: Paul asked for prayer for an open door for the word, not for his many personal needs. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-4/

**v. 4**
- Gill: the mystery was hidden in Old Testament types and shadows. Paul could make it plain as a minister, for God only, by his Spirit, makes it manifest in a spiritual, experimental, and saving way. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/colossians/4.htm
- Guzik: Paul wanted to keep making the gospel clear even if it meant more chains. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-4/
- Chrysostom: Paul means speaking very boldly and holding nothing back. He says Paul's chains make him more visible, not less. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230310.htm

**v. 5**
- Ellicott: the parallel in Ephesians 5:15 is about guarding against excess within. Here, wisdom watches for outside dangers and makes full use of outside opportunities. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/4.htm
- Gill: "outsiders" means unbelievers. Believers may still deal with them in trade and ordinary life, but should act inoffensively, so the gospel isn't spoken against and outsiders aren't hardened. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/colossians/4.htm
- Chrysostom ties this to Jesus' words "wise as serpents, harmless as doves." Christians shouldn't give outsiders any handle against them, or start quarrels that have nothing to do with preaching. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230311.htm

**v. 6**
- Ellicott hears an echo of Mark 9:50. He grants that salt can mean protection against corrupt talk, but thinks the context points to a ready answer for outsiders, like 1 Peter 3:15. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/4.htm
- Gill reads "with grace" as speech *about* grace, and also speech made in a gracious way. Salt makes speech wholesome and keeps it from corruption. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/colossians/4.htm
- Guzik, citing Barclay, takes "salt" as wit and charm. Christians shouldn't make the faith sound dull and sanctimonious. https://enduringword.com/grace-and-salt/
- Chrysostom: salt keeps graciousness from sliding into flattery. Different people should be answered differently. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230311.htm

**v. 7–8**
- Chrysostom: Paul left news to Tychicus partly to keep the letter short and partly to raise Tychicus's standing. Each title Paul gives him is a reason to trust him. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230311.htm
- Gill: Tychicus came from Asia (Acts 20:4). By tradition he was one of the Seventy and later bishop of Chalcedon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/colossians/4.htm
- Guzik's commentary, quoting F.F. Bruce, says the words about Tychicus are almost identical to Ephesians 6:21–22, so he probably carried that letter too. (I found this only in a Portuguese copy of Enduring Word.) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/por/tew/colossians-4.html

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: calling Onesimus "faithful and beloved" and "one of you" is a striking comment on the slaves-and-masters teaching just before. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/4.htm
- Guzik: Paul calls him a brother, not an escaped slave, which shows how the gospel changes relationships and identity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-4/
- Chrysostom: by saying "one of you," Paul makes the Colossians proud of Onesimus instead of ashamed. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230311.htm

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: Aristarchus came from Thessalonica and first appears in the Ephesus riot (Acts 19). This is Mark's first mention since Paul refused to take him because he had deserted them at Perga (Acts 15:38). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/4.htm
- Guzik: Aristarchus kept turning up with Paul in hard times. William Ramsay suggested he became Paul's slave so he could travel with him to Rome. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-4/
- Chrysostom: "welcome him" means welcome him with special attention, which shows Mark's standing. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230311.htm

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: nothing more is known of Justus. He suggests that the Jewish believers who opposed Paul out of envy (Philippians 1) explain why only three Jewish co-workers stood by him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/4.htm
- Guzik cites Adam Clarke: if Peter had been in Rome, he would surely have been on this list. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-4/
- Chrysostom guesses Justus was a Corinthian. He says those who share in the trials share in the kingdom. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230311.htm

**v. 12–13**
- Ellicott: "mature and fully assured" may answer the false teachers' claim to a superior perfection. Epaphras prays that every believer may have that maturity, based on God's revealed will. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/4.htm
- Guzik: prayer is hard work. Epaphras prayed well because he cared well. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-4/
- Gill: Epaphras was from Colossae and one of their ministers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/colossians-4.html

**v. 14**
- Ellicott: calling Luke "the beloved physician" suggests he was with Paul as both doctor and friend, since prison must have hurt Paul's health. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/4.htm
- Guzik: this is the only verse that tells us Luke was a doctor. (Portuguese copy of Enduring Word.) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/por/tew/colossians-4.html

**v. 15 (debated: Nympha's gender)**
- The manuscripts say "his house," "her house" or "their house." Ellicott preferred "their" and treated the name as a man's, Nymphas. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/4.htm
- NET Bible note (modern scholarship): The harder reading is certainly αὐτῆς, and thus Nympha should be considered a woman. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=col&chapter=4&verse=15
- The Pulpit Commentary notes the Greek form of the name could be male or female. https://biblehub.com/colossians/4-15.htm
- Bible Hub's Q&A: most modern scholars, citing Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus (two of the oldest Bible manuscripts), conclude the host was a woman. https://biblehub.com/q/who_was_nympha_in_the_bible.htm
- Translations follow the split: KJV, NKJV and Douay-Rheims have "his"; ESV, NIV, NASB and the Catholic New American Bible have "her." https://biblehub.com/colossians/4-15.htm
- Guzik: early churches met in homes, and several smaller groups made up one city church. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-4/

**v. 16 (debated: "the letter from Laodicea")**
- Ellicott: the verse shows how the apostles' letters were first read aloud and then passed around, which is how they came to be accepted as Scripture. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/4.htm
- Sam Storms (charismatic): it was most likely Paul's letter to Laodicea, not one written to Paul, and not Philemon. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/the-public-reading-of--lost--scripture--4:16-
- Ligonier (Reformed): the letter seems to be one Paul wrote to the believers in Laodicea. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/final-words-colossae
- The commentators who say "Ephesians": Coffman (as a circular letter) and Barclay, who calls it the most common explanation. Constable and Matthew Henry instead think it is a lost letter. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/colossians/4-16.html
- Bible.org (Utley) also says probably Ephesians, noting Marcion called Ephesians "the letter to the Laodiceans." https://bible.org/seriespage/colossians-4
- Ellicott, Vincent and Adam Clarke all call the surviving Latin "Epistle to the Laodiceans" a forgery. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/colossians/4-16.htm and https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-4/

**v. 17**
- Guzik: the message comes through the church, not from Paul directly, so Archippus would know his ministry was wanted. Quoting Clarke, it is encouragement rather than a rebuke. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-4/
- Chrysostom: Archippus seems to have held some office in the church. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230301.htm
- Ellicott: we can't tell whether he served in Colossae or Laodicea. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/colossians/4.htm

**v. 18**
- Gill: Paul signed in his own hand to guard against forged letters. "Remember my chains" urges them to hold to the gospel, endure suffering and pray for him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/colossians-4.html
- Guzik: the chains are not a plea for sympathy but a sign of his authority to speak God's truth. Ending with "grace" fits a letter written against a works-based heresy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/colossians-4/
